newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Gold- Hedging in state of limbo.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Gold- Hedging in state of limbo.

text.p: The slight rise in the gold price back towards US$380.00 does not mean Australian miners will be rushing to unwind forward positions or take on new ones.

The high level of forward positions held by miners in Australia and other countries, particularly South Africa, have been cited as inadvertently capping the gold price by providing a transparent price years into the future.
The Australian dollar gold price has fallen sharply to around A$480.00 an ounce due to the stronger local currency and a lower U.S. gold price, Macquarie Equities said in a report.
The recent lowering of interest rates also has reduced the Australian dollar gold contango, hence the appeal for hedging, it said.
"Local producers have been delivering a high proportion of of production into forward sales during this period," Macquarie said.
Meanwhile, several producers, including Placer Pacific Ltd, Plutonic Resources Ltd and Newcrest Mining Ltd have brought back large forward positions.
"The net impact is that the hedging levels of local producers is falling and a period of top-up hedging activity appears inevitable as soon as any price rally occurs," Macquarie said.
Brokerage firm J.B. Were & Son said in its latest commodities forecast that the Australian and South African currencies maintained a relative constant parity to the U.S. dollar in 1995.
However, it said, the picture changed earlier this year, with the collapse of the Rand and strengthening of the Australian dollar.

"The higher Rand price may tempt further selling in South Africa, but the picture in Australia is likely to have an opposite effect, with little opportunity for producers to lock in an acceptable spot price," it said.
Meanwhile, new concerns that the International Monetary Fund is finally ready to sell a potential five million ounces of gold to fund loans to developing countries are being downgraded.
"Even if they did sell gold, they wouldn't flood the market," said Mark Fremantle, senior gold trader for Rothschild Australia Ltd.
Keith Goode, analyst for Bell Securities Ltd of Australia, argues in Bell's latest report that the IMF sale has been overdone.

"The sale is only required fronm 2000 to 2004, when the IMF has a shortfall of US$3.5 billion to finance continuation of its ESAF (Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility) and participation in multilateral debt relief for poor countries," he said.

EMU (European Monetary union) sales in 1999 would probably be larger than five million ounces (156 tonnes) if the European Central Bank decided that a smaller gold holding was needed to defend effectively one currency.
Any such sales from the IMF or the EMU are expected to be fed into the market, probably by selling to Asian banks, so as not to overly disrupt the gold market and price, Goode said.
